tasks.question: CR-2311 rotated the mesh certificate authority. What does the step that decides whether a rotation is safe to start actually compare?

attempts.text: The step that decides whether a rotation is safe to start compares the shortest remaining leaf certificate lifetime across every counted service against the rotation window. If the shortest remaining lifetime is less than the rotation window, the rotation should not start because it would cause leaf certificates to expire before they can be re-issued. This comparison ensures the rotation timing is safe to avoid service disruption [1][7].

citations.title: Change record CR-2311: rotate the mesh certificate authority
heading_path: Change record CR-2311: rotate the mesh certificate authority
citations.quote:
## How it was done

The operator followed **RB-207** end to end and did not deviate. The step that
decides whether a rotation is safe to start is the one that compares the
shortest remaining leaf lifetime against the rotation window; this change record
does not restate it, because a procedure copied into a change record is a
procedure that stops being updated.

citations.title: RB-207: rotating the mesh certificate authority
heading_path: RB-207: rotating the mesh certificate authority
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Take the service count from the mesh control plane. Do not use the inventory
   label: a service missing its label is a service that will not be counted and
   will not be rotated.

2. Read the shortest remaining leaf lifetime across every counted service.

3. **Compare that lifetime against the rotation window.** If the shortest
   remaining lifetime is less than the window, stop: a rotation started now will
   expire leaves before they re-issue. The window is recorded in the platform
   limits reference and is not restated here.

4. Publish the new root, then trigger re-issue in batches of ten services.

5. Verify every counted service is serving a leaf signed by the new root before
   retiring the old one.

tasks.question: What is the mesh rotation window that RB-207 step three compares against?

attempts.text: The mesh rotation window that RB-207 step three compares against is six hours. A rotation may not begin if the shortest remaining leaf lifetime is below this six-hour window. This is recorded in the platform limits reference, which RB-207 refers to but does not restate explicitly in the runbook itself [2][6][3].

citations.title: Platform limits reference
citations.quote:
## Certificates

The mesh rotation window is **six hours**. A rotation may not begin if the
shortest remaining leaf lifetime is below it.

Leaf certificates are issued for 72 hours and re-issued at one third of
remaining life. The root is valid for one year.

tasks.question: CR-2311's pre-flight count reported 39 services. How many should it have reported?

attempts.text: CR-2311's pre-flight count reported 39 services, but it should have reported 41 services. The discrepancy was due to two services being excluded from the mesh inventory by a label typo, which caused the pre-flight count to be lower than the actual number of services [1][3][4].

citations.title: Change record CR-2311: rotate the mesh certificate authority
heading_path: Change record CR-2311: rotate the mesh certificate authority
citations.quote:
## What went wrong

Two services missed the window and served an expired leaf for nine minutes. Both
had been excluded from the mesh inventory by a label typo, so RB-207's
pre-flight count reported 39 services rather than 41.

citations.title: Change record CR-2311: rotate the mesh certificate authority
heading_path: Change record CR-2311: rotate the mesh certificate authority
citations.quote:
## What changed

The service mesh certificate authority was rotated on 2026-07-02 during the
Thursday change window. All 41 services re-issued leaf certificates against the
new root within the rotation window.

citations.title: Platform limits reference
citations.quote:
## Mesh

The control plane counts 41 services. Batch size for re-issue is ten; a larger
batch has been tried and saturates the issuing service.

Specifically, for an expired leaf certificate on a single service, RB-208 is the right procedure, not RB-207 [1][2].

tasks.question: Why did RB-207 step one tell the operator not to use the inventory label, and what happened in CR-2311 when it was used?

attempts.text:
RB-207 step one instructed the operator not to use the inventory label because a service missing its label would not be counted and therefore would not be rotated. Instead, the service count should be taken from the mesh control plane to ensure all services are included in the count [4].

In CR-2311, when the inventory label was used, two services were excluded from the mesh inventory due to a label typo. This caused RB-207's pre-flight count to report 39 services instead of the actual 41. As a result, two services missed the rotation window and served an expired leaf certificate for nine minutes [7]. After this incident, the pre-flight count was changed to be taken from the mesh control plane rather than from the inventory label [5].

citations.title: RB-207: rotating the mesh certificate authority
heading_path: RB-207: rotating the mesh certificate authority
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Take the service count from the mesh control plane. Do not use the inventory
   label: a service missing its label is a service that will not be counted and
   will not be rotated.

2. Read the shortest remaining leaf lifetime across every counted service.

3. **Compare that lifetime against the rotation window.** If the shortest
   remaining lifetime is less than the window, stop: a rotation started now will
   expire leaves before they re-issue. The window is recorded in the platform
   limits reference and is not restated here.

4. Publish the new root, then trigger re-issue in batches of ten services.

5. Verify every counted service is serving a leaf signed by the new root before
   retiring the old one.

The batch size of ten likely balances the need to manage the rotation process in manageable chunks while ensuring system stability during the transition [6].

heading_path: RB-207: rotating the mesh certificate authority
citations.quote:
## When to use this

A scheduled root rotation, or an emergency rotation after a suspected key
compromise. For an expired *leaf* certificate on a single service, this is the
wrong procedure and RB-208 is the right one.

citations.title: Platform limits reference
citations.quote:
## Change windows

The Thursday change window is four hours, 22:00 to 02:00 UTC. A change expected
to exceed it needs the change advisory board, not an operator's judgement.

citations.title: RB-207: rotating the mesh certificate authority
heading_path: RB-207: rotating the mesh certificate authority
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Take the service count from the mesh control plane. Do not use the inventory
   label: a service missing its label is a service that will not be counted and
   will not be rotated.

2. Read the shortest remaining leaf lifetime across every counted service.

3. **Compare that lifetime against the rotation window.** If the shortest
   remaining lifetime is less than the window, stop: a rotation started now will
   expire leaves before they re-issue. The window is recorded in the platform
   limits reference and is not restated here.

4. Publish the new root, then trigger re-issue in batches of ten services.

5. Verify every counted service is serving a leaf signed by the new root before
   retiring the old one.
